## Responsibility

The dispatch control plane converts one semantic Assignment into one governed
execution attempt. It resolves target, capability, provider/model/tier,
soul/profile, mechanism, adapter, policy checks, result channel, and runtime
metadata.

It does not choose the Work lifecycle transition or invent a semantic operation.

## Flow

```txt
Assignment
  -> policy resolver
  -> executor/target resolution
  -> governance and egress checks
  -> mechanism/adapter selection
  -> execution capability set
  -> Run creation and launch
  -> settlement/result collection
  -> RunResult normalization
```

`execution capability set` is a declared step, not a derived one. A mechanism
having been selected does not tell the Run what that mechanism can and cannot
do, so an executor declares it: how the prompt reaches the worker, what
permission posture it runs under and what confinement that posture requires,
what counts as a receipt, and whether the mechanism can be observed or
contacted at all. A capability the mechanism does not have is refused by name
rather than silently degraded, and a capability reachable in one execution
mode but not the other has to say so (ADR-010 §3).

## Routing Identities

The dispatch core recognizes exactly two target identities. No other name
resolves a Run target.

```txt
capability   — abstract behavior promise, resolved through
               runner.capabilities.<capability> (prefer/overrides), then
               runner.executors.<id>.for[]
executor-id  — explicit concrete implementation override, naming a
               runner.executors.<id> entry directly
```

`purpose` is not a third identity. It is compatibility terminology for
capability. The `--for <purpose>` CLI flag and the `purpose`/`for` parameter
names threaded through `src/runner/dispatch/plan.mjs` and
`src/runner/dispatch/resolve.mjs` (`resolveExecutorIdForPurpose`,
`resolveExecutorAndOverrides(cfg, executorIdOrPurpose)`) all name a capability
value, resolved against the same `runner.capabilities` catalog an explicit
capability selector would use. `compileDispatchPlan()`'s
`selector.type: 'purpose'` denotes a capability-shaped request, not a separate
ontology; nothing downstream branches on `purpose` as a concept distinct from
capability. Renaming these call sites internally is compatibility work
(tracked as Slice D/E in the normalization plan above), not a semantic
change — `--for`, `--work`, and `--assignment` stay supported at the CLI/API
adapter layer.

`job` is not a routing identity. ADR-004 reserves the term for a possible
future scheduler; where it appears (e.g. in logs), it names a caller's
execution-request label, never a target this control plane resolves against.
A `Run` (see the [Assignment/Run/RunResult Contract](../contracts/assignment-run-runresult.md))
is one concrete execution attempt for an Assignment — it is not a job or
operation identity either.

Work, workflow, stage, operation, taskSpec, skill, and protocol context are
component-outer. A caller in that layer may derive a capability or an
explicit executor-id from them before entering this control plane; none of
them becomes a third resolvable identity inside dispatch core. See
Component-Outer Boundary Note below.

## Contracts

These three contracts are canonical for this control plane. They are
additive over the current implementation, not a replacement of it — see the
Implementation Status line under each for what is real today versus still
Slice D/E scope in the normalization plan.

### DispatchRequest (outer → core)

```json
{
  "target": { "kind": "capability | executor", "value": "code:implement" },
  "policy": {
    "minTier": "standard",
    "preferExecutor": "agy-herdr",
    "fallbackExecutors": ["codex-herdr"],
    "preferPersona": "code-reviewer",
    "visibility": "headless"
  },
  "provenance": {
    "source": "workflow-operation",
    "domain": "coding",
    "workflow": "feature",
    "stage": "executing",
    "operation": "implement-item",
    "taskSpec": "implement-item",
    "skill": "fgos-coding-implement"
  }
}
```

Rules:

- `target.kind: capability` resolves through `runner.capabilities` and
  executor `for[]` bindings.
- `target.kind: executor` is an explicit concrete override and remains
  visible as an override — it must not silently discard a requested
  capability's provenance.
- `provenance` is explanatory/audit metadata, not an extra route key.
- Work/workflow/task/skill objects never cross this boundary as semantic
  resolver input; they are read by the component-outer caller only, before
  a DispatchRequest is built.
- An unavailable capability is a valid resolution result (`mechanism:
  "unavailable"`), not malformed config.

**Implementation status.** No single typed `DispatchRequest` object exists
yet. `compileDispatchPlan()`'s options bag
(`executorId | for | work | assignment | stage | needsSoul |
hasLiveTaskAccess | caller | cliOverride | options`) is the de facto request
shape today — untyped, and `work`/`assignment` are resolved to a
capability/executor-id *inside* `plan.mjs` rather than by the caller before
the boundary. Introducing a normalized `DispatchRequest` helper near
`plan.mjs` without changing `compileDispatchPlan`'s role as the sole
execution chooser is Slice D scope.

### PolicyPatch

One validated shape at every declared scope (runner/default, definition,
node, operation, role, actor, Work, Assignment, human/CLI, governance) — see
the [FlowDefinition Contract](../contracts/flow-definition.md#policypatch)
for the accepted schema. Dispatch does not define a second policy shape; it
consumes the same one.

```txt
runner/default
→ definition/protocol
→ operation/taskSpec
→ role
→ actor/persona
→ Work constraints
→ Assignment
→ trusted human/CLI override
→ governance
```

Merge rules (already accepted and enforced):

- tier constraints accumulate monotonically — a weaker layer cannot lower a
  stronger required tier;
- executor preference is most-specific-wins, subject to registration and
  governance;
- provider family derives from the selected registered executor, never from
  a raw selector string;
- literal model/executor names are not portable workflow/protocol data — a
  *portable* definition expresses `minTier`/`capabilities` only;
- provenance records the winning scope for every resolved field, as
  `{field: {value, source: {scope, id}}}`.

**Implementation status.** Implemented. `resolveAssignmentDispatchPolicy()`
(`src/runner/dispatch/assignment-policy.mjs`) implements this exact
precedence and provenance shape. `assertNoPortableExecutorPin()`
(`src/runner/coordination/session-engine.mjs`) already rejects a literal
`preferExecutor` declared at a portable definition/role/actor/operation
scope. `fallbackExecutors` remains `reserved-not-executed`: recorded and
validated, never automatically dispatched as failover.

### DispatchPlan (core → runtime)

```json
{
  "requestedTarget": { "kind": "capability", "value": "code:implement" },
  "requestedCapability": "code:implement",
  "selectedExecutor": "agy-herdr",
  "bindingSource": "capability.prefer",
  "providerModel": "gemini",
  "tier": "standard",
  "model": "<resolved-from-policy>",
  "mechanism": "out-of-process",
  "invocation": { "via": "cli", "adapter": "herdr-spawn" },
  "governance": {},
  "provenance": {}
}
```

An explicit executor override remains visible as an override; it must not
silently replace the requested capability's own provenance.

**Implementation status.** Implemented for dispatchable plans.
`compileDispatchPlan()` (`src/runner/dispatch/plan.mjs`) returns the legacy
selector/mechanism fields plus `bindingSource`, `tier`, `model`,
`providerModel`, structured field-level `provenance`, and the complete
merged `policy`. It delegates those policy fields to
`resolveAssignmentDispatchPolicy()` rather than re-deriving them, and
`assignment-runner.mjs` now reads `compiledPlan.policy` directly instead of
calling the policy resolver a second time.

For a real Assignment, policy resolution failure or a
decided-executor-versus-policy-executor mismatch remains a hard
`RunnerConfigError`. For a non-Assignment compatibility request
(`decide --for`, `decide <executor-id>`, `decide --work`), `plan.mjs`
synthesizes the smallest policy object needed for observability:
`preferExecutor` is the already-selected executor, and capability
`overrides.providerModel`/`overrides.model`/`overrides.tier`/
`overrides.rigorOverrides` are folded into the synthesized policy so the
reported model/tier matches the same capability-default path used by
execution. If that synthesized policy would disagree with an explicit caller
override, the plan stays dispatchable and records
`policy.executor-mismatch-ignored`; the optional policy fields are left
unset rather than turning a legacy `decide` probe into a thrown error.

Governance-blocked and genuinely unavailable plans also leave
`tier`/`model`/`providerModel`/`provenance`/`policy` unset so they never
publish a partial policy for a Run that will not launch.

`selector.type: 'purpose'` in the current implementation corresponds to
`requestedTarget.kind: 'capability'` in the target contract above (see
Routing Identities). It is a compatibility label on the public shape, not a
semantic third identity.

## Executor Kinds

An executor is not assumed to be an agent. `runner.executors.<id>.kind` is
one of `agent | tool` (`src/runner/dispatch/config.mjs`,
`EXECUTOR_KINDS`) — orthogonal to the invocation mechanism
(`invocations[].via`, one of `cli | task | mcp | api`). A `tool`/MCP-only
executor (e.g. `gitnexus`, `invocations: [{via: "mcp"}]`) is never spawned
as a subprocess: `resolveExecutorConfig()`'s own Gate B3 throws rather than
silently falling through to the global CLI executor when a caller asks an
MCP-only executor to resolve for CLI dispatch. This is how impact-analysis
tools like GitNexus participate in dispatch as executors without pretending
to be agents — the same control plane, the same capability/executor-id
routing, a different declared mechanism.

## Component-Internal Ownership

The Dispatch And Execution Engine owns exactly these authorities. No other
component performs any of them; this control plane performs none of the
Component-Outer Boundary Note's responsibilities.

1. **Request normalizer** — accepts only a normalized capability/executor
   target plus PolicyPatch/provenance; performs no Work graph traversal.
2. **Capability binding resolver** — resolves capability aliases, `prefer`,
   and executor `for[]` declarations (`resolveExecutorAndOverrides`).
3. **Executor registry resolver** — resolves a literal executor-id to its
   concrete invocation/tool/agent shape (`resolveExecutorConfig`).
4. **Policy resolver** — `resolveAssignmentDispatchPolicy`/
   `mergePolicyStack`; owns provider/model/tier derivation and provenance.
5. **Governance resolver** — checks egress/provider/executor/content
   constraints (cross-provider gate, `allowCrossProvider`, `carries`).
6. **Mechanism resolver** — decides in-process/out-of-process/unavailable
   and MCP/tool handback (`decideDispatchMechanism`,
   `decideExecutorDispatchMechanism`).
7. **DispatchPlan compiler** — `compileDispatchPlan()`; joins the prior
   decisions into one plan. Remains the sole execution chooser.
8. **Run runtime/adapters** — creates, launches, observes, settles, and
   retries a Run without choosing semantic operation
   (`assignment-runner.mjs`, `transport.mjs`, `herdr-round.mjs`).

Forbidden dependencies for all eight:

- no `Work` lifecycle mutation (`pick`, `return`, `claim`, `take`): enforced by boundary grep tests (`test/runner/dispatch-reconciliation-import-graph.test.mjs`). Work driving orchestration lives exclusively in Work Driver (`src/runner/loop.mjs`, `src/runner/fanout-batch.mjs`);
- no event store append (`appendEvent`): audit dispatch logging is isolated to `src/runner/dispatch-log.mjs` outside dispatch core;
- no workflow/stage/task/skill lookup: dispatch core contains no Work lookup implementations. Work capability lookups (`executorIdForWork`, `resolveCapabilityIdentityDetails`, `resolveCapabilityIdentity`, `buildPrompt`) are housed in dedicated leaf compatibility module `src/runner/work-compat.mjs` (registered as `infra` in architecture manifest) with zero imports into dispatch core; `src/runner/dispatch/resolve.mjs` and `prepare.mjs` provide backward-compatible re-exports without importing `workflow-stage-graphs` or `operation-choice.mjs`, consumed by pre-existing callers (`plan.mjs` for `compileDispatchPlan({work})` and `cli.mjs` for `spawnWorker`). All 13 strictly decoupled dispatch core modules contain zero `workflow-stage-graphs` imports, and boundary tests enforce that strict core modules cannot import Work lookup symbols or `work-compat.mjs` (verified by `test/runner/dispatch-reconciliation-import-graph.test.mjs`);
- no semantic operation choice;
- no direct protocol/skill/domain executor launch;
- no RunResult confidence decision (owned by the Run Result Evaluator);
- no provider/model selection outside the policy resolver (item 4);
- no second private dispatch path for a coordination or domain harness —
  `cohort-planner.mjs` is the one confirmed exception, and it only *re-reads*
  `resolveExecutorConfig`/`resolveAssignmentDispatchPolicy` for a
  pre-dispatch feasibility check; it never spawns and never bypasses them.

## Component-Outer Boundary Note

Work Driver, Coordination Engine/FlowDefinition, Domain Harness, and
Host/CLI/API callers derive a capability or explicit executor-id plus a
PolicyPatch and provenance, then hand a DispatchRequest to this control
plane. None of them calls `resolveExecutorConfig` or launches an executor
directly. `dispatchDeclaredOperation()`
(`src/runner/coordination/session-engine.mjs`) is the concrete example
today: it composes a full scoped policy stack (runner → definition →
operation → role → actor) and passes the winning provenance to
`resolveAssignmentDispatchPolicy` via `cliOverride.policyProvenance`, rather
than re-deriving policy itself. Full component-outer ownership (Work Driver,
FlowDefinition/operation, domain harness, host CLI/API selector
compatibility) is documented in the normalization plan's Slice C scope, not
duplicated here.

## Governance

- Executor identifiers must resolve through configured/approved targets.
- Cross-provider/model/tier dispatch must remain explicit and auditable.
- Capability, role, soul/profile, privacy, and context-egress requirements must
  be resolved through policy rather than hard-wired to a Workflow.
- CLI spawn is an execution mechanism, not a governance bypass.
- Read-only/mutating policy must be checked before launch.
- Result and artifact locations must be bounded and attributable to the Run.
- Direct executor calls from protocol, Skill, coordinator, or domain-harness
  prose are invalid.

## Separation Of Concerns

```txt
planner     proposes a declared or dynamic semantic action
policy      validates legality, authority, bounds, and selected domain rules
builder     creates Assignment
resolver    produces governed DispatchPlan
dispatcher  launches and observes Run
normalizer  creates RunResult
caller      consumes evidence and invokes authorized lifecycle behavior, if any
```

Planning may be agent-led, declared, or domain-assisted. Dispatch does not care
which source proposed the validated Assignment and must not create separate
runtime paths for them. A CoordinationSession or a declared
`CoordinationProtocol` FlowDefinition (see
[ADR-008](../decisions/ADR-008-coordination-session-and-mission-deferral.md),
[ADR-009](../decisions/ADR-009-flow-definition-shared-ir-and-typed-profiles.md))
is one more caller of this same flow: a Cohort Planner may emit actor policy
inputs, but it resolves and dispatches exactly one Assignment at a time
through this control plane — it may not spawn an executor directly or read
sibling Assignment state.

The detailed redesign source remains a
[proposal](../proposals/dispatch-control-plane-redesign.md) until its unresolved
target-state sections are reconciled with implementation.

## Source Inventory

| Layer | Modules | Responsibilities & Boundaries |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dispatch Core | `src/runner/dispatch/**` (`cli.mjs`, `plan.mjs`, `resolve.mjs`, `prepare.mjs`, `settlement.mjs`, `reconcile-cli-spawn.mjs`, `herdr-reconcile.mjs`, `proof-helpers.mjs`, `assignment-runner.mjs`, `confinement/**`, `transport.mjs`, `herdr-round.mjs`, `brief.mjs`, `assignment.mjs`, `runtime-inspection.mjs`) | Execution allocation, plan compilation, executor commands, confinement, and adapter execution. Strictly zero references to `pick`, `return`, `claim`, or `appendEvent`. |
| Work Driver Compatibility | `src/runner/work-compat.mjs` | Leaf compatibility module (registered as "infra" in architecture manifest) housing Work Driver compatibility lookup implementations (`executorIdForWork`, `resolveCapabilityIdentityDetails`, `resolveCapabilityIdentity`, `buildPrompt`) with zero imports into dispatch core; consumed by `plan.mjs`/`cli.mjs` via compatibility re-export. |
| Stage Operation Selection | `src/runner/dispatch/operation-choice.mjs` | Bridge for stage operation selection (`chooseStageOperation`, `executeDriverOperationChoice`) consuming hardened RunResult. |
| Work Driver | `src/runner/loop.mjs`, `src/runner/fanout-batch.mjs` | Work item lifecycle orchestration, batch fan-out driving (`pick -> executeExecutorCli -> return`), fail-safe settlement (`fgos return --to blocked`), and worker slots occupancy (`OccupancyPort`). |
| Audit Seam | `src/runner/dispatch-log.mjs` | Audit event logging (`logExecutorDispatch`) isolated from dispatch core. |
~~~~

+- `provenance` is explanatory/audit metadata, not an extra route key.
+- Work/workflow/task/skill objects never cross this boundary as semantic
+  resolver input; they are read by the component-outer caller only, before
+  a DispatchRequest is built.
+- An unavailable capability is a valid resolution result (`mechanism:
+  "unavailable"`), not malformed config.
+
+**Implementation status.** No single typed `DispatchRequest` object exists
+yet. `compileDispatchPlan()`'s options bag
+(`executorId | for | work | assignment | stage | needsSoul |
+hasLiveTaskAccess | caller | cliOverride | options`) is the de facto request
+shape today — untyped, and `work`/`assignment` are resolved to a
+capability/executor-id *inside* `plan.mjs` rather than by the caller before
+the boundary. Introducing a normalized `DispatchRequest` helper near
+`plan.mjs` without changing `compileDispatchPlan`'s role as the sole
+execution chooser is Slice D scope.
+
+### PolicyPatch
+
+One validated shape at every declared scope (runner/default, definition,
+node, operation, role, actor, Work, Assignment, human/CLI, governance) — see
+the [FlowDefinition Contract](../contracts/flow-definition.md#policypatch)
+for the accepted schema. Dispatch does not define a second policy shape; it
+consumes the same one.
+
+```txt
+runner/default
+→ definition/protocol
+→ operation/taskSpec
+→ role
+→ actor/persona
+→ Work constraints
+→ Assignment
+→ trusted human/CLI override
+→ governance
+```
+
+Merge rules (already accepted and enforced):
+
+- tier constraints accumulate monotonically — a weaker layer cannot lower a
+  stronger required tier;
+- executor preference is most-specific-wins, subject to registration and
+  governance;
+- provider family derives from the selected registered executor, never from
+  a raw selector string;
+- literal model/executor names are not portable workflow/protocol data — a
+  *portable* definition expresses `minTier`/`capabilities` only;
+- provenance records the winning scope for every resolved field, as
+  `{field: {value, source: {scope, id}}}`.
+
+**Implementation status.** Implemented. `resolveAssignmentDispatchPolicy()`
+(`src/runner/dispatch/assignment-policy.mjs`) implements this exact
+precedence and provenance shape. `assertNoPortableExecutorPin()`
+(`src/runner/coordination/session-engine.mjs`) already rejects a literal
+`preferExecutor` declared at a portable definition/role/actor/operation
+scope. `fallbackExecutors` remains `reserved-not-executed`: recorded and
+validated, never automatically dispatched as failover.
+
+### DispatchPlan (core → runtime)
+
+```json
+{
+  "requestedTarget": { "kind": "capability", "value": "code:implement" },
+  "requestedCapability": "code:implement",
+  "selectedExecutor": "agy-herdr",
+  "bindingSource": "capability.prefer",
+  "providerModel": "gemini",
+  "tier": "standard",
+  "model": "<resolved-from-policy>",
+  "mechanism": "out-of-process",
+  "invocation": { "via": "cli", "adapter": "herdr-spawn" },
+  "governance": {},
+  "provenance": {}
+}
+```
+
+An explicit executor override remains visible as an override; it must not
+silently replace the requested capability's own provenance.
+
+**Implementation status.** Implemented for dispatchable plans.
+`compileDispatchPlan()` (`src/runner/dispatch/plan.mjs`) returns the legacy
+selector/mechanism fields plus `bindingSource`, `tier`, `model`,
+`providerModel`, structured field-level `provenance`, and the complete
+merged `policy`. It delegates those policy fields to
+`resolveAssignmentDispatchPolicy()` rather than re-deriving them, and
+`assignment-runner.mjs` now reads `compiledPlan.policy` directly instead of
+calling the policy resolver a second time.
+
+For a real Assignment, policy resolution failure or a
+decided-executor-versus-policy-executor mismatch remains a hard
+`RunnerConfigError`. For a non-Assignment compatibility request
+(`decide --for`, `decide <executor-id>`, `decide --work`), `plan.mjs`
+synthesizes the smallest policy object needed for observability:
+`preferExecutor` is the already-selected executor, and capability
+`overrides.providerModel`/`overrides.model`/`overrides.tier`/
+`overrides.rigorOverrides` are folded into the synthesized policy so the
+reported model/tier matches the same capability-default path used by
+execution. If that synthesized policy would disagree with an explicit caller
+override, the plan stays dispatchable and records
+`policy.executor-mismatch-ignored`; the optional policy fields are left
+unset rather than turning a legacy `decide` probe into a thrown error.
+
+Governance-blocked and genuinely unavailable plans also leave
+`tier`/`model`/`providerModel`/`provenance`/`policy` unset so they never
+publish a partial policy for a Run that will not launch.
+
+`selector.type: 'purpose'` in the current implementation corresponds to
+`requestedTarget.kind: 'capability'` in the target contract above (see
+Routing Identities). It is a compatibility label on the public shape, not a
+semantic third identity.
+
+## Executor Kinds
+
+An executor is not assumed to be an agent. `runner.executors.<id>.kind` is
+one of `agent | tool` (`src/runner/dispatch/config.mjs`,
+`EXECUTOR_KINDS`) — orthogonal to the invocation mechanism
+(`invocations[].via`, one of `cli | task | mcp | api`). A `tool`/MCP-only
+executor (e.g. `gitnexus`, `invocations: [{via: "mcp"}]`) is never spawned
+as a subprocess: `resolveExecutorConfig()`'s own Gate B3 throws rather than
+silently falling through to the global CLI executor when a caller asks an
+MCP-only executor to resolve for CLI dispatch. This is how impact-analysis
+tools like GitNexus participate in dispatch as executors without pretending
+to be agents — the same control plane, the same capability/executor-id
+routing, a different declared mechanism.
+
+## Component-Internal Ownership
+
+The Dispatch And Execution Engine owns exactly these authorities. No other
+component performs any of them; this control plane performs none of the
+Component-Outer Boundary Note's responsibilities.
+
+1. **Request normalizer** — accepts only a normalized capability/executor
+   target plus PolicyPatch/provenance; performs no Work graph traversal.
+2. **Capability binding resolver** — resolves capability aliases, `prefer`,
+   and executor `for[]` declarations (`resolveExecutorAndOverrides`).
+3. **Executor registry resolver** — resolves a literal executor-id to its
+   concrete invocation/tool/agent shape (`resolveExecutorConfig`).
+4. **Policy resolver** — `resolveAssignmentDispatchPolicy`/
+   `mergePolicyStack`; owns provider/model/tier derivation and provenance.
+5. **Governance resolver** — checks egress/provider/executor/content
+   constraints (cross-provider gate, `allowCrossProvider`, `carries`).
+6. **Mechanism resolver** — decides in-process/out-of-process/unavailable
+   and MCP/tool handback (`decideDispatchMechanism`,
+   `decideExecutorDispatchMechanism`).
+7. **DispatchPlan compiler** — `compileDispatchPlan()`; joins the prior
+   decisions into one plan. Remains the sole execution chooser.
+8. **Run runtime/adapters** — creates, launches, observes, settles, and
+   retries a Run without choosing semantic operation
+   (`assignment-runner.mjs`, `transport.mjs`, `herdr-round.mjs`).
+
+Forbidden dependencies for all eight:
+
+- no `Work` lifecycle mutation (`pick`, `return`, `claim`, `take`): enforced by boundary grep tests (`test/runner/dispatch-reconciliation-import-graph.test.mjs`). Work driving orchestration lives exclusively in Work Driver (`src/runner/loop.mjs`, `src/runner/fanout-batch.mjs`);
+- no event store append (`appendEvent`): audit dispatch logging is isolated to `src/runner/dispatch-log.mjs` outside dispatch core;
+- no workflow/stage/task/skill lookup: dispatch core contains no Work lookup implementations. Work capability lookups (`executorIdForWork`, `resolveCapabilityIdentityDetails`, `resolveCapabilityIdentity`, `buildPrompt`) are housed in dedicated leaf compatibility module `src/runner/work-compat.mjs` (registered as `infra` in architecture manifest) with zero imports into dispatch core; `src/runner/dispatch/resolve.mjs` and `prepare.mjs` provide backward-compatible re-exports without importing `workflow-stage-graphs` or `operation-choice.mjs`, consumed by pre-existing callers (`plan.mjs` for `compileDispatchPlan({work})` and `cli.mjs` for `spawnWorker`). All 13 strictly decoupled dispatch core modules contain zero `workflow-stage-graphs` imports, and boundary tests enforce that strict core modules cannot import Work lookup symbols or `work-compat.mjs` (verified by `test/runner/dispatch-reconciliation-import-graph.test.mjs`);
+- no semantic operation choice;
+- no direct protocol/skill/domain executor launch;
+- no RunResult confidence decision (owned by the Run Result Evaluator);
+- no provider/model selection outside the policy resolver (item 4);
+- no second private dispatch path for a coordination or domain harness —
+  `cohort-planner.mjs` is the one confirmed exception, and it only *re-reads*
+  `resolveExecutorConfig`/`resolveAssignmentDispatchPolicy` for a
+  pre-dispatch feasibility check; it never spawns and never bypasses them.
+
+## Component-Outer Boundary Note
+
+Work Driver, Coordination Engine/FlowDefinition, Domain Harness, and
+Host/CLI/API callers derive a capability or explicit executor-id plus a
+PolicyPatch and provenance, then hand a DispatchRequest to this control
+plane. None of them calls `resolveExecutorConfig` or launches an executor
+directly. `dispatchDeclaredOperation()`
+(`src/runner/coordination/session-engine.mjs`) is the concrete example
+today: it composes a full scoped policy stack (runner → definition →
+operation → role → actor) and passes the winning provenance to
+`resolveAssignmentDispatchPolicy` via `cliOverride.policyProvenance`, rather
+than re-deriving policy itself. Full component-outer ownership (Work Driver,
+FlowDefinition/operation, domain harness, host CLI/API selector
+compatibility) is documented in the normalization plan's Slice C scope, not
+duplicated here.
+
+## Governance
+
+- Executor identifiers must resolve through configured/approved targets.
+- Cross-provider/model/tier dispatch must remain explicit and auditable.
+- Capability, role, soul/profile, privacy, and context-egress requirements must
+  be resolved through policy rather than hard-wired to a Workflow.
+- CLI spawn is an execution mechanism, not a governance bypass.
+- Read-only/mutating policy must be checked before launch.
+- Result and artifact locations must be bounded and attributable to the Run.
+- Direct executor calls from protocol, Skill, coordinator, or domain-harness
+  prose are invalid.
+
+## Separation Of Concerns
+
+```txt
+planner     proposes a declared or dynamic semantic action
+policy      validates legality, authority, bounds, and selected domain rules
+builder     creates Assignment
+resolver    produces governed DispatchPlan
+dispatcher  launches and observes Run
+normalizer  creates RunResult
+caller      consumes evidence and invokes authorized lifecycle behavior, if any
+```
+
+Planning may be agent-led, declared, or domain-assisted. Dispatch does not care
+which source proposed the validated Assignment and must not create separate
+runtime paths for them. A CoordinationSession or a declared
+`CoordinationProtocol` FlowDefinition (see
+[ADR-008](../decisions/ADR-008-coordination-session-and-mission-deferral.md),
+[ADR-009](../decisions/ADR-009-flow-definition-shared-ir-and-typed-profiles.md))
+is one more caller of this same flow: a Cohort Planner may emit actor policy
+inputs, but it resolves and dispatches exactly one Assignment at a time
+through this control plane — it may not spawn an executor directly or read
+sibling Assignment state.
+
+The detailed redesign source remains a
+[proposal](../proposals/dispatch-control-plane-redesign.md) until its unresolved
+target-state sections are reconciled with implementation.
+
+## Source Inventory
+
 | Layer | Modules | Responsibilities & Boundaries |
 | --- | --- | --- |
 | Dispatch Core | `src/runner/dispatch/**` (`cli.mjs`, `plan.mjs`, `resolve.mjs`, `prepare.mjs`, `settlement.mjs`, `reconcile-cli-spawn.mjs`, `herdr-reconcile.mjs`, `proof-helpers.mjs`, `assignment-runner.mjs`, `confinement/**`, `transport.mjs`, `herdr-round.mjs`, `brief.mjs`, `assignment.mjs`, `runtime-inspection.mjs`) | Execution allocation, plan compilation, executor commands, confinement, and adapter execution. Strictly zero references to `pick`, `return`, `claim`, or `appendEvent`. |
 | Work Driver Compatibility | `src/runner/work-compat.mjs` | Leaf compatibility module (registered as "infra" in architecture manifest) housing Work Driver compatibility lookup implementations (`executorIdForWork`, `resolveCapabilityIdentityDetails`, `resolveCapabilityIdentity`, `buildPrompt`) with zero imports into dispatch core; consumed by `plan.mjs`/`cli.mjs` via compatibility re-export. |
 | Stage Operation Selection | `src/runner/dispatch/operation-choice.mjs` | Bridge for stage operation selection (`chooseStageOperation`, `executeDriverOperationChoice`) consuming hardened RunResult. |
 | Work Driver | `src/runner/loop.mjs`, `src/runner/fanout-batch.mjs` | Work item lifecycle orchestration, batch fan-out driving (`pick -> executeExecutorCli -> return`), fail-safe settlement (`fgos return --to blocked`), and worker slots occupancy (`OccupancyPort`). |
-| Audit Seam | `src/runner/dispatch-log.mjs` | Audit event logging (`logExecutorDispatch`) isolated from dispatch core. |+| Audit Seam | `src/runner/dispatch-log.mjs` | Audit event logging (`logExecutorDispatch`) isolated from dispatch core. |
+~~~~
````

Diversity is not\n   decoration — it is a hedge against a single model's characteristic blind\n   spots and house style. If you cannot honestly say what independence the\n   diversity bought in this session, record that too.\n4. Respect configured policy and budget.\n5. Fall back, in order: another safe pair in the same provider family; then\n   the same pair in a fresh isolated assignment with a distinct prompt package.\n   Never fall back to \"the coordinator does it inline\".\n\nThen, for every actor, run the decision door before dispatch:\n\n  node src/runner/dispatch.mjs decide <safe-executor-id> --has-live-task-access\n\nand obey the answer:\n- \"in-process\": use your own live Agent/Task capability, but only if that exact\n  mechanism's confinement has been proven for this roster. An unproven\n  in-process boundary counts as no independent dispatch.\n- \"out-of-process\": run it through `node src/runner/dispatch.mjs execute` with\n  the immutable prompt file, tier, and cwd.\n- \"unavailable\": there is no independent dispatch for this actor. Record the\n  gap. Do NOT perform the role inline and present it as panel output.\n\nRecord, per actor: requested executor / tier / persona, the derived provider and\nmodel, whether tier materially changed the model on this executor, the immutable\nprompt path, and the run result path. If tier made no difference on a given\nexecutor, say so plainly — an unmaterial tier is honest information, not a\nfailure.\n\nDefault cognitive needs and tiers are in the role doctrine's routing roster.\nRead it once; do not re-derive it per session.\n\nMANUAL VISIBILITY IS PROMPT ISOLATION, NOT A RUNTIME GUARANTEE\n\nIn manual mode, \"the shapers could not see each other\" means exactly this: each\nshaper received its own prompt file containing the same frame and the same\nevidence, with no sibling output in it, and the critic received the proposals\nonly after every first pass had settled. That is prompt/package isolation. It is\nnot a runtime visibility window and must never be described as one. Say what it\nactually was.\n\nPERSISTENT STATE AND CRASH RECOVERY\n\nEverything a successor coordinator needs lives on disk. Nothing important lives\nin this conversation.\n\nUse:\n\n  <EVIDENCE_DIR>/\n    session.md            compact status board: case, phase, roster, next action\n    intake.md             the person's immutable words + case boundary\n    interpretation.md     lead advisor's reading, marked as interpretation\n    scout-report.md       investigator findings, including disconfirmations\n    decision-request.md   the one consolidated question packet, if any\n    human/<n>-person.md   the person's own words, verbatim, one file per turn\n    proposals/<role>.md   each shaper's independent proposal\n    critiques/<role>.md   attacks, per critic, per proposal\n    synthesis.md          the Decision Packet\n    explanation.md        Phase 8's human-facing explanation. One file; a later\n                          explanation is a new appended section, not a new file\n    dialogue/<n>-impact.md     lead advisor's reading of human turn <n>\n    dialogue/<n>-response.md   the panel's authorized response to human turn <n>\n    dispositions.md       driver dispositions AND dialogue authorizations,\n                          append-only, with rationale\n    redteam.md            the independent red-team's attacks, cited artifacts,\n                          and APPROVE / REVISE / INSUFFICIENT-EVIDENCE verdict\n    review.md             the reviewer's standalone assessment. A separate actor\n                          and a separate file; never merged into redteam.md, and\n                          neither reads the other's output before writing its own\n    rubric.md             the person's own assessment, then the evaluators'\n    prompts/<role>.md     immutable prompt packages, exactly as dispatched\n    runs/<ordinal>-<role>.json   dispatch decision + result per actor\n\nThese names are fixed, not suggestions. A coordinator must never have to invent\na filename mid-session: every path above has a matching prose template, under\nthe same name, in the artifact templates document. If you find yourself needing\nan artifact this tree does not name, that is a gap in the playbook — record it\nin session.md as a gap rather than quietly coining a filename a successor will\nnot know to look for.\n\nThe four layers of THE DIALOGUE TURN PROTOCOL map onto four of these paths and\nnever share one: human/<n>-person.md (the person's words), dialogue/<n>-impact.md\n(the lead advisor's reading), dispositions.md (your authorization),\ndialogue/<n>-response.md (the panel's response). Same ordinal <n> across all\nfour, so a turn can be reassembled end to end months later.\n\nRules that make recovery actually work:\n\n1. Write the artifact before you act on it. If the interpretation is not on\n   disk, the interpretation does not exist and no shaper may be dispatched\n   against it.\n2. session.md always names the current phase and the single next action in\n   imperative form (\"dispatch alternative shaper against frame v2\"). A\n   successor reads exactly this file first and needs no other orientation.\n3. Artifacts are append-only. A revised frame becomes frame v2 in a new\n   section; the old frame stays readable. Deleting superseded reasoning\n   destroys the only record of why the panel changed its mind, which is one of\n   the things this session exists to demonstrate.\n4. Prompt packages are immutable once dispatched. If a prompt was wrong,\n   dispatch a new one with a new ordinal; never edit a prompt that has already\n   run.\n5. Every artifact names its author role and provenance in its own header. An\n   unattributed artifact is unusable evidence.\n\nRECOVERY HANDOFF — WHAT A FRESH COORDINATOR DOES\n\nGiven only EVIDENCE_DIR and no chat history:\n\n1. Read session.md. It names the phase and next action.\n2. Read intake.md and the newest human/ turn. This is the ground truth of what\n   was actually asked and said. Read these before any panel artifact, so that\n   the panel's framing does not become your memory of the question.\n3. Read interpretation.md and dispositions.md. Now you know what the panel\n   believes and what the driver has authorized.\n4. Read only the artifacts the next action needs. Do not re-read every\n   proposal to feel oriented; that is how a resumed session drifts into\n   restarting.\n5. Check runs/ against session.md's roster: any actor with a prompt but no\n   result was interrupted mid-flight. Re-dispatch it under a new ordinal\n   rather than assuming its silence meant anything.\n6. Continue from the named next action. Do not re-run a completed phase merely\n   because you did not personally witness it. If you genuinely cannot trust a\n   phase's output, say so in session.md and re-run it deliberately, as a\n   recorded decision.\n\nA session that cannot survive this procedure is not finished, no matter how\ngood its recommendation is.\n\nTHE NINE-PHASE COGNITIVE LOOP\n\nNine phases, in order, with real backward edges. Phase 9 may reopen 3, 5, 6, or\n7; nothing else jumps backwards silently.\n\nEight of these phases are the panel's required doctrine. The ninth — Phase 1,\nIntake and Framing — is added deliberately, and here is the justification,\nbecause a phase count is not self-justifying:\n\n  Every downstream artifact is an interpretation of something. If the person's\n  own words are never frozen as an artifact of their own, before anyone reads\n  them charitably, then interpretation silently becomes the origin, and there\n  is nothing left to check later artifacts against. The invariant that \"the\n  original human input, the panel's interpretation, the recommendation, and the\n  human decision stay separate\" is unenforceable without a phase whose only job\n  is producing the first of those four. Intake is also what makes crash\n  recovery possible at all: a successor coordinator needs a version of the\n  question that predates the panel's opinion about it. So Phase 1 is not\n  ceremony bolted on to reach nine — it is the phase that makes the other eight\n  auditable.\n\nPHASE 1 — INTAKE AND FRAMING (coordinator)\n\nFreeze the ask. Copy the person's words into intake.md verbatim — including the\nvagueness, the hedges, and the parts that seem irrelevant. Do not clean up\ngrammar, do not merge two half-sentences into one crisp question, do not\ntranslate a symptom into a decision. The exact wording is evidence; a person who\nsays \"it's becoming difficult to evolve\" has told you something different from\n\"we need a pipeline abstraction\", and the difference is the whole case.\n\nAlso record: PROJECT_ROOT, who the person is and what authority they hold, what\nis genuinely undecided, what is explicitly out of bounds, and any constraint the\nperson volunteered.\n\nAll of that is transcription, not elicitation. Who the person is and what\nauthority they hold is copied from the PERSON input, exactly as the launcher\nfilled it — Phase 1 has no channel to the person and opens none. If PERSON is\nthin (\"the maintainer\"), that is what intake.md says, and every further detail\nabout their authority is Phase 3's job: CODEOWNERS, the commit history on the\npaths in question, repository permissions, who has merged changes here before,\nwho is named in the project's own decision records. Never turn an authority gap\ninto a question. \"Do you actually own this decision?\" is both answerable by\nscouting and unpleasant to be asked, which makes it the exact question SCOUT\nBEFORE ASK exists to prevent. If scouting cannot settle it and it is genuinely\nmaterial — the recommendation would differ depending on the answer — it becomes\none line in Phase 4's single Decision Request, alongside everything else, and\nnever a standalone interruption at intake.\n\nThen confirm the case boundary with yourself: is this actually undecided? If\nrepository evidence shows the decision was already made and the person is\nseeking ratification, that is a different and shorter session, and you say so.\n\nResolve the roster now, before opinions exist, so that routing cannot be\nretro-fitted to a conclusion.\n\nExit when intake.md exists, session.md names the roster, and no advisor has yet\nbeen dispatched.\n\nPHASE 2 — UNDERSTAND THE PERSON (lead advisor, dispatched)\n\nBefore understanding the problem, understand who has it. Infer, provisionally:\n\n- intent — what they are actually trying to achieve, which is often not what\n  they asked about;\n- vocabulary — the words they use for their own system, which the panel must\n  adopt rather than correct;\n- altitude — are they asking at the level of a module, a service boundary, a\n  team structure, or a product bet;\n- constraints — stated and implied, technical and organizational;\n- risk appetite — what they treat as an acceptable failure, inferable from what\n  they have already shipped and how they talk about past incidents;\n- decision burden — what makes this hard for them specifically. Is it\n  reversibility? Cost? A commitment to a colleague? Not knowing whether they\n  are allowed to choose?\n\nMark every inference with honest uncertainty. \"Probably\", \"I could not tell\",\nand \"this is a guess and it matters\" are required vocabulary here. An\ninterpretation that reads as confident throughout is almost certainly\noverconfident somewhere, and it will mislead every shaper downstream.\n\nThe output is interpretation.md, authored by the lead advisor through its own\ndispatch, clearly labelled as interpretation and never merged into intake.md.\n\nPHASE 3 — UNDERSTAND THE PROBLEM (context investigator, dispatched)\n\nGo look. Read the code, the structure, the configuration, the tests, the commit\nhistory, the issue tracker if reachable. Then:\n\n- distinguish symptom from cause. \"Evolution is hard\" is a symptom. The cause\n  might be coupling, might be missing tests, might be that two teams share a\n  file, might be that the person is the only one who understands it;\n- test the boundaries the person's framing assumes. If they framed it as \"one\n  pipeline or two\", check whether the real seam is somewhere else entirely;\n- seek disconfirming evidence deliberately. Write down the panel's early\n  hypothesis and then go looking for what would prove it wrong. A scout report\n  that only confirms the framing it was given has not scouted;\n- record what you could not determine, and what would determine it.\n\nThe scout report is evidence, not opinion. It cites paths and observations. An\ninvestigator that recommends an architecture has left its lane.\n\nPHASE 4 — ASK RELUCTANTLY BUT CLEARLY (coordinator + lead advisor)\n\nApply SCOUT BEFORE ASK. If nothing survives, record \"no user question needed\"\nwith the reasoning, and proceed — this is a good outcome, not a skipped step.\n\nIf something survives, the lead advisor drafts one Decision Request: every\nquestion, each with why it matters, what the panel will assume if unanswered,\nand which options the answer would eliminate. You authorize it; you do not\nauthor it. Then it goes to the person once, and the panel keeps working on\neverything that does not depend on the answer while it waits. A pending question\nnever idles the whole panel.\n\nPHASE 5 — DIVERGE HONESTLY (shapers + constraint advocate, dispatched, isolated)\n\nDispatch the system shaper, the alternative shaper, and the constraint advocate\nagainst the same frame and the same evidence, in separate prompt packages, with\nno sibling output. Different provider families where the roster allows.\n\nRequirements on the set of candidates, which you enforce before proceeding:\n\n- at least one materially smaller intervention than the obvious one, and an\n  honest no-build / do-nothing path with its real consequences. \"Do nothing\" is\n  frequently the correct architecture decision and is almost never proposed\n  unless someone is required to propose it;\n- no straw options. A candidate that exists to lose is a lie about the option\n  space and it corrupts every comparison downstream. If a shaper cannot make an\n  alternative credible, it says so and drops it rather than weakening it;\n- materially different, not cosmetically different. Two proposals that differ\n  only in naming or in which layer holds a helper are one proposal. Send them\n  back;\n- every shaper states, before any critic sees the proposal, what evidence\n  would change its own position. This is not optional and it is not a\n  formality: a shaper that cannot name its own falsification criteria has\n  produced advocacy, not design. Record these criteria with a timestamp so it\n  is checkable that they preceded the critique.\n\nPHASE 6 — DEBATE CLAIMS (critic + advocate + shapers, dispatched)\n\nReveal all proposals to the critic together, after every first pass has settled.\nThe critic attacks assumptions, consequences, and evidence — never the actor.\n\"The shaper is wrong\" is not an attack; \"this assumes read volume stays under X,\nand the commit history shows it tripled in six months\" is.\n\nEach attack states what evidence would settle it. Shapers may respond, may\nconcede, and may revise — and a shaper that changes its mind and explains why\nhas done the single most valuable thing that happens in this phase. Record the\nchange and the reason; do not quietly replace the old position.\n\nWhere the disagreement is genuinely about values rather than facts — speed\nversus reversibility, simplicity versus optionality — say so. Pretending a value\ndisagreement is a factual one is how panels manufacture false consensus.\n\nPHASE 7 — CONVERGE WITHOUT FLATTENING (synthesizer, dispatched)\n\nThe synthesizer reads the whole ledger and produces the Decision Packet. It must:\n\n- recommend one option. A panel that lists three options with balanced pros and\n  cons has handed the work back to the person and charged them for it. Be\n  decisive;\n- calibrate that decisiveness honestly. State confidence, and state what it\n  rests on. \"High confidence given the observed query patterns; low confidence\n  about team capacity, which we could not verify\" is a better output than\n  uniform confidence;\n- preserve minority positions and unresolved objections as first-class content,\n  with the name of who held them and what would settle them. Dissent that\n  survives into the packet is the panel working correctly, not a defect to be\n  smoothed;\n- preserve missing or failed actors, stale evidence, and the revision each\n  input was based on;\n- never introduce a new argument. The synthesizer integrates; if it finds a gap\n  that needs a new position, it says so and the coordinator reopens Phase 5 or\n  6 rather than letting synthesis quietly become authorship.\n\nPHASE 8 — EXPLAIN FOR OWNERSHIP (lead advisor, dispatched)\n\nTranslate the packet into the person's own vocabulary and altitude. This phase\nexists because a recommendation the person cannot defend to their own colleagues\nis worthless even when it is correct.\n\nThe explanation must convey: what this means concretely for their system; what\nbecomes easier and what becomes harder; what the first reversible step is; under\nwhat observed conditions they should reverse it; what the panel is uncertain\nabout; and — explicitly — which part of this decision remains theirs and cannot\nbe delegated to the panel. Name that last part. People routinely under-notice\nthat they still hold the decision, and a panel that lets them drift into\ncompliance has failed even if the architecture is right.\n\nThe output is explanation.md, authored by the lead advisor through its own\ndispatch. It is the only artifact written to be read by the person rather than\nby the panel, and it is a separate file from synthesis.md on purpose: the packet\nis the panel's record, the explanation is the handover, and collapsing them\nproduces a document that serves neither. If a later dialogue turn changes what\nthe person needs to understand, append a new revision section to explanation.md;\ndo not start a second explanation file.\n\nPHASE 9 — STAY IN DIALOGUE (coordinator, bounded)\n\nThe person responds. Record their words in human/<n>-person.md, dispatch the\nlead advisor to write dialogue/<n>-impact.md, record your authorization in\ndispositions.md, and persist whatever the panel says back in\ndialogue/<n>-response.md — every turn, including the ones that feel too small to\nfile. A one-line clarification answered in chat and never written down is the\nmost common way an otherwise recoverable session becomes unrecoverable, because\nthe next coordinator cannot tell whether the person was answered or ignored.\n\nClassify the turn and act:\n\n- clarification — they want something explained. Answer. This does not reopen\n  anything and does not consume a reopen cycle;\n- challenge — they dispute a claim. Defend it with evidence, or concede. A\n  panel that cannot be moved by a good objection was never advising;\n- new context — they supply a fact the panel did not have. This is material:\n  reopen the phase it actually affects (often 3, sometimes 5) and say plainly\n  which conclusions it changes and which it does not;\n- request for an alternative — they want an option the panel did not produce.\n  Reopen Phase 5 for that option specifically, through a real shaper dispatch;\n- request for a composition — they want parts of two options. Reopen Phase 7\n  with that composition as an explicit candidate; do not let the coordinator\n  improvise the merge;\n- decision — record it, in their words, in human/, and stop advising;\n- deferral — record it as an honest outcome with what they are waiting for.\n  An intentional deferral with named trigger conditions is a successful\n  session, not a failed one.\n\nReopens are bounded, predeclared, and append-only. No advisor is deleted, no\nearlier evidence is rewritten, and no reopen invents a new phase. If the panel\ngenuinely cannot reach consensus after a reopen, say so without defensiveness\nand hand the person the honest disagreement — that is more useful than a\nmanufactured agreement and they will know the difference.\n\nTHE DIALOGUE TURN PROTOCOL\n\nFour things are involved in every dialogue turn, and they never merge:\n\n1. The person's immutable words. Stored verbatim in human/<n>-person.md,\n   attributed to the person, never edited, never summarized in place. If the\n   input arrived by voice, paste, or relay, record the channel.\n2. The lead advisor's interpretation of those words. A separate artifact\n   (dialogue/<n>-impact.md), a separate dispatch, explicitly labelled as\n   interpretation, carrying its own uncertainty. This is where \"I think they\n   mean X\" lives. It is never written into the person's file and never quoted\n   as if the person said it.\n3. The driver's authorization. You, the coordinator, decide what the panel is\n   permitted to do in response — which phase reopens, which actors run, what\n   bounds apply. This is an authorization, not an opinion about the\n   architecture, and it is recorded in dispositions.md.\n4. The panel's response, in dialogue/<n>-response.md: what the dispatched\n   advisors produced under that authorization, and what it changed. It states\n   which authorization it was produced under, so nobody has to reconstruct\n   whether a response exceeded what was permitted. A clarification answered\n   with no reopen still gets this file — one paragraph and the citation it\n   rests on is a complete response.\n\nThe ordinal <n> is shared across all four. Turn 3 is human/3-person.md,\ndialogue/3-impact.md, the dispositions.md entry naming turn 3, and\ndialogue/3-response.md — never renumbered, never reused.\n\nThe reason these are kept apart is blunt: it must remain possible, months later,\nto check whether the panel answered what the person actually asked. Merge the\nlayers and that check becomes impossible, and the failure mode it guards against\n— a panel confidently answering its own paraphrase — is both common and\ninvisible from the inside.\n\nTwo hard rules follow:\n\n- You may never author a human turn. Not as a placeholder, not as a\n  best-guess, not as a clearly-labelled simulation. If no person is available,\n  park with a consolidated request naming the packet, the exact interaction\n  needed, and everything that can continue without it.\n- Your authorization is not a decision. Authorizing the panel to reconsider\n  option B is not choosing option B, and no artifact may present it as one.\n\nDRIVER DISPOSITION\n\nEvery finding, objection, and unresolved point gets exactly one disposition,\nrecorded in dispositions.md with rationale and evidence reference:\n\n- accepted — valid, and it changes the recommendation or the packet;\n- answered — already addressed by existing evidence; cite it;\n- mitigated — valid, not eliminated, and the packet now carries the mitigation\n  and the residual risk;\n- deferred — valid but out of scope for this decision; name what it belongs to;\n- unresolved — valid, unsettled, and it goes to the person as visible dissent.\n  This is a legitimate outcome. Do not convert an unresolved objection into a\n  \"mitigated\" one to make the packet look tidier;\n- invalidated-by-evidence — a specific observation refutes it; cite the\n  observation, not your own reasoning.\n\nYou must NOT disposition without another advisor's evidence when the disposition\nturns on a technical claim about PROJECT_ROOT. \"Invalidated-by-evidence\" and\n\"answered\" both assert a fact about the system; if you have not been shown that\nfact by an advisor who looked, you are not dispositioning, you are opining\ninside an authority role. Dispatch the investigator and wait. The one thing you\nmay always disposition alone is scope — deferral is an authority call, not a\ntechnical one.\n\nThe full doctrine, with worked examples of each disposition done well and done\nbadly, is in the role doctrine document.\n\nSTOP CONDITIONS\n\nStop, preserve everything, and emit one consolidated request when one of the\nfollowing holds. Each carries the marker you would actually see — a stop\ncondition you cannot detect is decoration, and these are written so that you\ncan check them rather than sense them.\n\n- No real person is available for a Decision Dialogue turn the session\n  genuinely requires. Marker: a Decision Request has been sent, the phase\n  ledger shows every non-dependent line of work completed, and there is no\n  turn in human/ answering it. The tell that you are about to violate a bound\n  instead of stopping: you catch yourself drafting \"they would probably say\".\n- The panel cannot be independently dispatched, so a real panel is\n  impossible. Marker: `dispatch.mjs decide` returned \"unavailable\" for the\n  shaper roles, or every attempted dispatch failed with no run result.\n- Fewer than two safe executor/provider bindings exist, making an\n  independent panel structurally impossible rather than merely less diverse.\n  Marker: count the distinct provider families you can actually reach on the\n  roster right now. One is a stop; two is a thin panel you disclose and run.\n- The case turns out to be already decided, and the person is seeking\n  ratification rather than advice. Markers, any one of which is enough to\n  check deliberately and at least two of which together are decisive: the\n  work is already in PROJECT_ROOT's history (a branch, a spike, a dependency\n  added, a migration written) for the option their wording assumes; a\n  decision record, RFC, or issue already names the choice as made; the\n  person's own words presuppose one option throughout and ask only about\n  execution of it (\"how should we structure the plugin registry\" rather than\n  \"should we have one\"); or their stated question has an axis that the\n  repository shows was closed months ago. Worked example: the case reads\n  \"how do we roll out the new pipeline abstraction safely\" and `git log`\n  shows `common/pipeline_base.py` already merged, imported by both paths, and\n  under active commit. That is not an architecture question with an answer\n  outstanding; it is a rollout question, and the honest service is to say\n  which one you found and offer the shorter session.\n- The question is not actually an architecture question — it is a\n  product, legal, staffing, or budget decision wearing architecture clothes.\n  Marker: run the substitution test before stopping. Write down what each\n  candidate architecture would change about the system itself, then ask whether\n  the person's stated pain would still be there afterwards. If every\n  candidate leaves the pain untouched, the pain has a different cause. The\n  sharper form: name who could resolve this by deciding something, without\n  any code changing. Worked examples — \"should we split the service\" where\n  the scout finds one repository, one deploy, and two teams who cannot agree\n  on ownership is a staffing decision; \"can we build this on the free tier\"\n  is a budget decision; \"must we keep raw ticks for seven years\" is a legal\n  question a specialist can inform but the panel cannot decide; \"should this\n  be one product or two\" is a product decision. Say so plainly; noticing this\n  is one of the more useful things a panel does, and it is worth more to the\n  person than a well-argued answer to the wrong question.\n- The evidence needed to distinguish the top two candidates cannot be\n  obtained without mutating PROJECT_ROOT or running something the bounds\n  forbid. Marker: the critic's decision-changing attack states a settling\n  observation, and the investigator reports that observation requires a\n  write, a deploy, a production query, or a load test. Name the spike and\n  stop; do not substitute an opinion for the measurement.\n- Proceeding would require the panel to invent a fact about the person's\n  obligations. Marker: a claim load-bearing for the recommendation has no\n  source in PROJECT_ROOT and no source in anything the person said, and the\n  only way to fill it is to assume. Worked examples: \"they presumably have a\n  30-day retention requirement\"; \"the SLA is probably 99.9%\"; \"their\n  customers would accept an hour of downtime\"; \"the security team will sign\n  off on this\". Each of those is a sentence about a commitment nobody in the\n  session has seen. Note the difference from a safe default — a default is\n  something you state, the person can override by not replying, and the panel\n  can recover from if it is wrong. An invented obligation is none of those:\n  being wrong about it means the recommendation was never viable. If it fails\n  that test, it goes in the Decision Request; if there is no person to send\n  it to, this stop condition fires. See the narrow immediate-ask exception in\n  SCOUT BEFORE ASK — it exists for exactly this class of fact.\n\nDo not stop because one optional specialist is unavailable, because one\nnon-material unknown remains, because the panel disagrees internally, or because\nthe recommendation is uncomfortable.\n\nFINAL OUTPUT PER SESSION\n\nReport concisely:\n- the case, in the person's words and in the panel's frame, side by side;\n- the roster actually used, with requested and derived provider/model/tier per\n  actor, and one honest sentence on what the diversity bought;\n- what the investigation changed about the framing;\n- whether a question was asked, and if not, why not;\n- the candidates, including the smaller and no-build paths;\n- the recommendation, its confidence, and what it rests on;\n- surviving dissent and unresolved objections, named;\n- the dialogue turns and what each changed;\n- the outcome: decision, deferral with triggers, or honest no-consensus;\n- artifact paths, and confirmation that a fresh coordinator could resume.\n\nNever report a decision the person did not make.\n```"
  },
